items.title: Aggregation Dispersion: An Information-Geometric Diagnostic of Oversmoothing in Graph Neural Networks
items.body: Message-passing neural networks (MPNNs) learn node representations by iteratively aggregating information from neighbors, but stacking too many layers causes all representations to converge, an effect known as oversmoothing. We propose a geometric perspective on this phenomenon. At each depth $k$, the propagation operator assigns to every node $v$ a walk distribution $p_v^{(k)}$, a probability distribution over source nodes. These walk distributions form a point cloud on the probability simplex, whose contraction to a single point characterizes complete mixing of the propagation operator, and thus oversmoothing. To measure this contraction, we use the Fisher-Rao metric, the unique Riemannian metric on the simplex invariant up to scale under sufficient statistics, whose scaled chordal distance under the square-root embedding $p \mapsto \sqrt{p}$ is the Hellinger distance. The resulting diagnostic, the aggregation dispersion $D_k$, is the variance of the embedded point cloud on the unit sphere. We prove that: (i) $D_k = 0$ if and only if the $k$-th step propagation matrix has rank one, a necessary and sufficient condition for complete operator mixing; (ii) $D_k$ is non-increasing with depth; (iii) the spectral gap of the propagation matrix controls the rate of this decay; and (iv) for contractive MPNNs, the aggregation dispersion upper-bounds the representation dispersion up to graph- and initialization-dependent constants. Across 14 model configurations and 11 datasets, $D_k$ attains the highest mean absolute Pearson correlation with test accuracy across depths among eight diagnostics ($|r| = 0.721$, using log-transformed diagnostic values), numerically comparable to the post-training effective rank ($|r| = 0.688$), while requiring no training.

items.title: Similarity-Constrained Reweighting for Complex Query Answering on Knowledge Graphs
items.body: Machine learning models for Complex Query Answering (CQA) on knowledge graphs estimate the likelihood of answers that are not reachable via direct traversal. Recent work has proposed extending such queries with soft entity constraints, which require the target variable to be similar or dissimilar to specified sets of entities. We study a more general formulation where similarity constraints are specified on an arbitrary variable in a query, and introduce SCORE: a computationally efficient and interpretable method for incorporating similarity constraints on an arbitrary variable of a query. SCORE is based on a lightweight and interpretable score adjustment function that only requires tuning two hyperparameters on a validation set. Our experiments show that SCORE effectively incorporates preferences while maintaining strong query answering performance. It significantly improves ranking quality when constraints apply to the target variable and performs effectively in the more general case involving constraints on intermediate variables, and its performance remains robust when applied to several existing methods for CQA. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/dfdazac/score.

items.title: Ladybird's first alpha release
items.body:
Ladybird is an astonishingly ambitious project: a new browser, in 2026, with its own implementation of most of the key components - HTML parsing, CSS engine, layout, JavaScript, even WebAssembly. It still uses a few external components - things like HarfBuzz for text shaping, Skia for 2D graphics, ffmpeg for video, and SQLite for the things you do with SQLite. Everything else is part of Ladybird, or code brought in from Ladybird's even more ambitious predecessor project SerenityOS.

This morning the Ladybird project released their first alpha, which means you can now install the browser (on macOS or Linux) without having to compile it yourself!

I've been trying it out today, and it's very impressive. It feels fast, the UI is lightweight and intuitive, and most of the websites I've tried to load in it have worked as they should. It looks like this (showing my video-compressor tool):

Here's the process tree after I opened six tabs in one window and another tab in a second window (generated by this script, thanks Claude):

Ladybird (72925) [240 MB]
└── Hub (72926) [61 MB]
├── RequestServer (72927) [29 MB]
├── ProcessReaper (72928) [1 MB]
├── Compositor (72930) [123 MB]
├── RequestServer (72953) [36 MB]
├── WebContent (72984) [819 MB]
├── MediaServer (73006) [118 MB]
├── VideoDecoderServer (73007) [20 MB]
├── WebContent (73052) [144 MB]
├── WebContent (73057) [73 MB]
├── WebContent (73073) [166 MB]
├── WebContent (73094) [70 MB]
├── WebContent (73112) [116 MB]
├── RequestServer (73113) [27 MB]
└── WebContent (73185) [60 MB]
Ladybird runs different tabs in different processes, an isolation mechanism used by most browsers (well, technically Chrome uses a process-per-site).

I tried Ladybird against several of my more advanced tool examples - like the video-compressor shown above, which runs ffmpeg compiled to WebAssembly. I had it resize its own screenshot using my image-resize tool. It happily runs my Pyodide REPL (Python compiled to WebAssembly) too.

The one thing I tried that didn't work was Datasette Lite, which runs Pyodide in a complicated arrangement of service workers and web workers. Attempting to start Datasette Lite displays this error:

undefined is not a function (evaluated from 'navigator.serviceWorker.startMessages')

I filed an issue about this, then found a FIXME annotation in the source code.

The October explosion

The project has been leaning heavily into coding agents this year. On February 23, 2026 Andreas Kling published Ladybird adopts Rust, with help from AI, describing how they ported parts of their LibJS JavaScript engine from C++ to 25,000 lines of Rust in two weeks using Claude Code and Codex.

Here's the GitHub contributions chart for Ladybird over the past twelve months:

That uptick in October corresponds to the landing of a wealth of big improvements.

This Month in Ladybird — October 2026 describes what happened. In addition to moving style and layout to their own thread, landing a new JavaScript JIT, and replacing their C++ with Cranelift WebAssembly engine with new code that achieved a 7x boost on the JetStream 3 WASM benchmark, they gained 75,650 new passes on the ~2.25 million subtest web-platform-tests suite, beating Safari!

How did they do that? Coding agents:

Most of that gain came in five days, from about 2.12 million on October 22 to about 2.18 million on October 27. We pointed AI coding agents at WPT and asked them to fill in missing functionality. They made lots of small fixes, and those added up. Our biggest gains for the month were about 30,000 in /css and 10,000 in /editing.

I'm interested in what models they are using here - I know Andreas uses Codex and Claude Code, but I haven't seen him talk about specific model versions. Claude Opus 5.5 came out on September 22, 2026 and Claude Fable 5.2 on November 9, 2026 (after that window). I'd love to know what they were using for that huge leap in the last week of October.

Should you use Ladybird?

Here's what Andreas says about Ladybird's suitability for use as a daily browser:

This is an alpha, so some websites won’t work, and it will crash sometimes. When that happens, tell us! You can report a broken site from inside the browser. After a crash, you can read the crash report and decide whether to send it. Our privacy policy has the details.

We want security nerds to hack it! A new browser gets hacked, over and over, and that’s part of the process, so we make no promises about security today. When you pwn us, please tell us how so we can harden Ladybird!

Given how hard it is to secure a web browser, and the hostility of the environment they operate in, I won't be using Ladybird to sign into GitHub or Gmail or any of my other sensitive accounts.

I'm going to keep it around for anonymous browsing though, partly to participate in the testing efforts but mainly because it gives me a glimmer of optimism to see a promising new entrant in the stagnant browser engine market start to grow its wings.

items.title: datasette-charts 0.1a0
items.body:
Release: datasette-charts 0.1a0

I've been thinking about this problem for over a year now, but on Sunday I finally fired up Claude Fable 5.2 to build an initial prototype. The prototype went so well that this is now a full plugin.

You can try it out in Datasette Lite here. It looks like this:

The new charts plugin works against any table or arbitrary SQL query in Datasette. It defines several different chart types (using vendored D3, Observable Plot, and topojson-client), each with a set of heuristics for identifying when they might be a good match for a specific set of rows.

Those suggestion thumbnails at the top are actual visualizations driven by the data, and selecting one pulls up the full chart along with tools for modifying it. You can also manually construct a chart from scratch.

As with other Datasette visualization plugins, the current state of your chart is persisted in a #fragment in the URL - so you can bookmark charts or share them with others.

The most important feature is that the charts take all rows into account. Previous charting plugins like datasette-vega would only show charts for the current page of results, generally up to 100 rows.

The new plugin compiles each chart to a SQL query that aggregates across the entire result set (potentially millions of rows) using GROUP BY, time bucketing, and window functions. Each query returns a result capped at 5,000 rows, suitable for display on the chart. The plugin uses sampling to help suggest charts for larger tables without evaluating the full result set.

I'm really happy with this initial release of the plugin. It's still very much an alpha, but it's the closest I've got to the dream of Datasette helping visualize data with as little required direction from the user as possible.

items.title: [AINews] Jensen Is Back! and OpenAI Shows Its Pretraining Curve, joined by Microsoft
items.body:
Congrats to Sierra on tripling last year’s $10B valuation, and to Z.ai for releasing GLM 5.4, their first looped transformer following Thinking Machine’s much smaller Inkling Mini 2 from last week. However all these are outshone by today’s twin title stories…

Jensen Huang is back. Eleven days after announcing his resignation, Nvidia announced his return as CEO, president and member of the Board of Directors.

View post on X ↗

The board voted unanimously after more meetings with Jensen on Sunday and said it received input from senior U.S. officials (aka the Treasury Secretary and the President dialing into the board meeting). Colette Kress remains CFO, the independent directors’ investigation continues, and Jensen’s Senate hearing is still due in 8 days. Nvidia also formed a board committee for national security and export control.

As Matt Levine points out, with the firing AND the rehiring by this board with involvement from the government, the investigators are now being put in a position of having had the outcome somewhat predetermined for them, because both have demonstrated that they did not need to wait for any further evidence to come to light.

OpenAI put its pretraining loss curve on the record. In Perplexity and Intelligence, Chief scientist Jakub Pachocki plotted base-model log-perplexity back to GPT-3.5 (on their internal held-out coding dataset… which has notable caveats):

View post on X ↗

Think of it as how surprised the model is by the next token on a held-out dataset. Lower is better. GPT-3.5 was around 0.99 and GPT-4 around 0.91. When OpenAI put a model around 0.76 (GPT6 Astra) to work on open math problems, hundreds of frontier math problems started falling quickly. Pachocki extrapolates that another jump in capabilities could come around 0.68–0.70.

This is all in context of pacing the frontier. Pachocki proposes that labs agree on a first limit to development and spell out what would let them cross it, such as a successor to chain-of-thought monitoring. Microsoft’s Mustafa Suleyman gave the first win by cosigning and joining in, running MAI-2 Base on OpenAI’s evaluation set and reporting 0.819. We’d need at least a couple more top labs to join this effort for it to gather steam as a real self-regulatory limit, most notably of course, Anthropic.

AI Twitter Recap

OpenAI Publishes Its Pretraining Perplexity History and Proposes Shared Development Limits

The disclosure: Jakub Pachocki's essay "Perplexity and Intelligence" publishes five years of OpenAI base-model log-perplexity on a fixed held-out dataset. It argues for industry-wide limits based on perplexity and other measurements, with further progress gated on milestones in understanding and monitoring AI behavior, such as a successor to chain-of-thought (CoT) monitors (essay thread).
Policy framing: Sam Altman quoted the proposal for a first common limit with concrete exit criteria (quote). He tied it to the standards commitments in the White House Accords (accords).

Endorsements: Greg Brockman highlighted the warning that alignment progress is unlikely to keep pace with pretraining acceleration (gdb). Mark Chen called the numbers formerly "sensitive IP" and asked other labs to disclose their key metrics (markchen90).

Claimed findings: Losses below 0.8 coincided with emergent capabilities in cybersecurity and mathematics (excerpt).
Thresholds and timing: OpenAI expects further "transformative capabilities" in the ~0.68–0.7 window and describes a steep acceleration in 2026 (summary).

Internal model: An unreleased internal model already sits below GPT-6.2 Astra. Pachocki says pretraining could see an "avalanche" like the recent one in math as soon as 2027 (scaling01).

Community extrapolations (unofficial): Dan Hendrycks infers ~3–5×/yr compute-efficiency gains since GPT-4, possibly 100×+ this year (hendrycks). One fit, using the internal model at 0.732 against 0.761 for the released model, reaches 0.70 between January and March 2027 (fits).

Microsoft joins: With OpenAI's permission, Microsoft AI reported MAI-2 Base at 0.819 on OpenAI's eval set. It shares OpenAI's tokenizer and lands in GPT-5.6 Sol base-model territory. Mustafa Suleyman suggested bits-per-byte for future cross-lab comparisons (mustafasuleyman).
Open-model mapping: Elie Bakouch used MAI as a bridge to place open models on OpenAI's curve (plot). He labels the further chaining through Inkling bpb a "very weak approximation" (details).

Lucas Beyer's caveat: Inkling's held-out codebase may be largely agent-generated, which would make bridge-based placements look too optimistic (giffmana).

Methodological critiques: Critics raised several confounds:
Tokenizer bias: Common limits could favor OpenAI over Anthropic because of tokenizer differences (davidmanheim).

Post-training compute: Post-training likely accounts for more than 75% of FLOPs, so pretraining perplexity may be the wrong pacing metric (stochasticchasm).

Synthetic data: Part of the steep curve may come from a growing share of model-generated pretraining data (Azaliamirh).

Missing context: Without model sizes or compute figures, it is hard to separate scaling from algorithmic progress (Grad62304977).

OpenAI's response: Staff say the eval is fixed over time and excludes model-generated code (johnohallman). Will Depue added that it is "held out, frozen, tokenizer agnostic" (willdepue).

Pressure on other labs: Several researchers asked OpenAI to release the held-out set (oneill_c; DimitrisPapail).
Anthropic's redactions: Anthropic redacted pretraining metrics from its METR report (eliebakouch), prompting calls to publish them (_NathanCalvin).

Third-party verification: METR offered to verify pause or compute-allocation claims under its standard terms (ChrisPainterYup).

Frontier Model and Product Launches: Gemini 4 Neon, GPT-6.2 Sol, Claude Ship

Gemini 4 Neon: Google positions Neon between Carbon (hardest long-horizon work) and Hydrogen (fast execution), aimed at complex coding and enterprise workflows (Google).
Leaderboard results: Neon claims several top spots:
LiveBench 2.0: #1 at 87.4, versus 84.9 for both Claude Fable 5.2 and GPT-6.2 Astra, at roughly a quarter of Fable's cost per task (LiveBench).

AI Chess Leaderboard: #1 at 1924 Elo (chess).

Arena text: Google holds the top three, with Carbon at 1527, Argon at 1520 and Neon at 1513 (Arena).

Adoption signals: OpenRouter spend on Google models exceeded OpenAI's for the first time since June (OpenRouter).
Perplexity traffic: Neon is compounding +10.6%/day in Ask and +15%/day in Computer. Aravind Srinivas says this is organic switching from Opus 5.5 and Sol 6.2, not default routing (growth; clarification).

Access rules: Gemini subscriptions work only through the Antigravity binary. T3 Code is allowed because it wraps Antigravity; shims such as Pi are not (theo; Google confirmation).
Quota changes: Antigravity quotas were reset. Pro users get Carbon, and Hydrogen opens to all users (_mohansolo).

Workspace: Neon is rolling out to Workspace customers in the Gemini app (OfficialLoganK).

Hydrogen pricing: Hydrogen costs $1.50 per million input tokens. It scores 51 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, against 50 for Argon, and 57% on Terminal-Bench 4.1 (dl_weekly).

API features: New file slicing lets agents upload once and pay only for the pages, cells or clips Gemini inspects (googledevs). Function results can now return documents, audio and video natively (_philschmid).

젠슨 황이 돌아왔습니다. 사임 발표 11일 만에 Nvidia는 그가 CEO, 사장 및 이사회 이사로 복귀한다고 발표했습니다.

X에서 게시물 보기 ↗

이사회는 일요일 젠슨과의 추가 회의 후 만장일치로 투표했으며, 미국 고위 관계자들(재무부 장관과 대통령이 이사회 회의에 전화로 참여하는 것을 의미)로부터 의견을 받았다고 밝혔습니다. Colette Kress는 CFO로 남아 있으며, 독립 이사들의 조사는 계속되고, 젠슨의 상원 청문회는 아직 8일 남았습니다. Nvidia는 또한 국가 안보 및 수출 통제를 위한 이사회 위원회를 구성했습니다.

Matt Levine이 지적했듯이, 정부의 개입으로 이사회에 의해 해고되었다가 다시 고용된 상황에서, 조사관들은 결과가 어느 정도 미리 결정된 위치에 놓이게 되었습니다. 왜냐하면 양측 모두 추가 증거가 나올 때까지 기다릴 필요가 없다는 것을 보여주었기 때문입니다.

OpenAI는 사전 학습 손실 곡선을 공개했습니다. 수석 과학자 Jakub Pachocki는 "Perplexity and Intelligence"에서 GPT-3.5까지(그들의 내부 held-out 코딩 데이터셋에 대한… 주목할 만한 주의사항이 있는) 기본 모델의 로그 퍼플렉시티를 그렸습니다.

X에서 게시물 보기 ↗

이는 모델이 held-out 데이터셋에서 다음 토큰에 대해 얼마나 놀라는지를 나타낸다고 생각하면 됩니다. 낮을수록 좋습니다. GPT-3.5는 약 0.99였고 GPT-4는 약 0.91이었습니다. OpenAI가 약 0.76(GPT6 Astra)의 모델을 사용하여 공개 수학 문제에 적용했을 때, 수백 개의 최전선 수학 문제가 빠르게 해결되기 시작했습니다. Pachocki는 0.68–0.70 부근에서 또 다른 능력의 도약이 올 수 있다고 추정합니다.

이 모든 것은 최전선을 조절하는 맥락에서 이루어집니다. Pachocki는 연구소들이 개발에 대한 첫 번째 한계에 동의하고, chain-of-thought 모니터링의 후속작과 같이 이를 넘어서기 위해 무엇이 필요한지 명확히 밝힐 것을 제안합니다. Microsoft의 Mustafa Suleyman은 OpenAI의 평가 세트에서 MAI-2 Base를 실행하고 0.819를 보고하며 이에 동의하고 참여함으로써 첫 번째 승리를 거두었습니다. 이것이 진정한 자율 규제 한계로 추진력을 얻으려면, 가장 중요한 Anthropic을 포함하여 최소한 두세 개의 주요 연구소가 이 노력에 참여해야 합니다.

Backblaze B2 후원

데이터가 계획보다 빠르게 증가하고 있다면, 비즈니스와 함께 성장하고, 테라비트 스케일 처리량으로 플래시와 GPU를 공급하며, 이그레스 비용을 부과하지 않는 스토리지가 필요합니다.
Backblaze B2는 20년 동안 용량 계층 스토리지를 제공했으며, 6엑사바이트 이상을 관리하고 있으며, 선도적인 네오클라우드, 연구소 및 생성 AI 회사에서 신뢰받고 있습니다.
성장은 걱정할 일이 되어서는 안 됩니다. 저희는 여러분이 만들고 있는 무엇이든 담을 공간이 있습니다.

OpenAI, 사전 학습 퍼플렉시티 기록 공개 및 공유 개발 한계 제안

공개 내용: Jakub Pachocki의 에세이 "Perplexity and Intelligence"는 OpenAI 기본 모델의 고정된 held-out 데이터셋에 대한 5년간의 로그 퍼플렉시티를 공개합니다. 이 에세이는 퍼플렉시티 및 기타 측정값을 기반으로 한 산업 전반의 한계를 주장하며, chain-of-thought(CoT) 모니터의 후속작과 같이 AI 행동 이해 및 모니터링의 이정표를 통해 추가 진행을 제한할 것을 제안합니다(에세이 스레드).
정책 프레임워크: Sam Altman은 구체적인 종료 기준을 가진 첫 번째 공통 한계 제안을 인용했습니다(인용문). 그는 이를 백악관 협정의 표준 약속과 연결했습니다(협정).

지지: Greg Brockman은 정렬 진행이 사전 학습 가속을 따라가지 못할 가능성에 대한 경고를 강조했습니다(gdb). Mark Chen은 이 수치들이 이전에 "민감한 IP"였다고 말하며 다른 연구소들에게 주요 지표를 공개할 것을 요청했습니다(markchen90).

주장된 발견: 0.8 미만의 손실은 사이버 보안 및 수학 분야에서 발현되는 능력과 일치했습니다(발췌).
임계값 및 시점: OpenAI는 ~0.68–0.7 범위에서 추가적인 "변혁적 능력"을 기대하며 2026년에 가파른 가속을 설명합니다(요약).

내부 모델: 아직 출시되지 않은 내부 모델은 이미 GPT-6.2 Astra보다 낮은 퍼플렉시티를 보입니다. Pachocki는 사전 학습이 2027년만큼이나 빨리 최근 수학 분야의 "눈사태"와 같은 상황을 볼 수 있다고 말합니다(scaling01).

커뮤니티 추정치(비공식): Dan Hendrycks는 GPT-4 이후 연간 ~3–5배의 컴퓨팅 효율성 증가를 추론하며, 올해는 100배 이상일 수도 있다고 합니다(hendrycks). 출시된 모델의 0.761에 대해 내부 모델을 0.732로 사용하여 하나의 적합을 시도하면 2027년 1월에서 3월 사이에 0.70에 도달합니다(fits).

Microsoft 참여: OpenAI의 허가하에 Microsoft AI는 OpenAI의 평가 세트에서 MAI-2 Base가 0.819라고 보고했습니다. 이 모델은 OpenAI의 토크나이저를 공유하며 GPT-5.6 Sol 기본 모델 영역에 해당합니다. Mustafa Suleyman은 향후 연구소 간 비교를 위해 bits-per-byte를 제안했습니다(mustafasuleyman).
공개 모델 매핑: Elie Bakouch는 MAI를 다리로 사용하여 공개 모델을 OpenAI의 곡선에 배치했습니다(플롯). 그는 Inkling bpb를 통한 추가 연결을 "매우 약한 근사치"라고 표현했습니다(세부 정보).

Lucas Beyer의 주의사항: Inkling의 held-out 코드베이스는 대부분 에이전트가 생성한 것일 수 있으며, 이는 다리 기반 배치를 너무 낙관적으로 보이게 만들 수 있습니다(giffmana).

방법론적 비판: 비평가들은 여러 가지 혼란스러운 요인을 제기했습니다:
토크나이저 편향: 공통 한계는 토크나이저 차이 때문에 Anthropic보다 OpenAI에 유리할 수 있습니다(davidmanheim).

사후 학습 컴퓨팅: 사후 학습이 FLOP의 75% 이상을 차지할 가능성이 높으므로, 사전 학습 퍼플렉시티는 잘못된 진행률 측정 지표일 수 있습니다(stochasticchasm).

합성 데이터: 가파른 곡선의 일부는 모델이 생성한 사전 학습 데이터의 비중 증가에서 비롯될 수 있습니다(Azaliamirh).

누락된 맥락: 모델 크기나 컴퓨팅 수치가 없으면 스케일링과 알고리즘 진행을 분리하기 어렵습니다(Grad62304977).

OpenAI의 답변: 직원들은 평가가 시간이 지남에 따라 고정되어 있으며 모델이 생성한 코드를 제외한다고 말합니다(johnohallman). Will Depue는 "held out, frozen, tokenizer agnostic"이라고 덧붙였습니다(willdepue).

다른 연구소에 대한 압력: 여러 연구원들은 OpenAI에 held-out 세트를 공개할 것을 요청했습니다(oneill_c; Di)
